Profit Growth, Data Centers, and Nuclear Power: "GS Engineering & Construction Is the Second-Preferred Stock in Construction" [Click eStock] On September 22, KB Securities maintained a 'Buy' investment rating on GS Engineering & Construction and raised its target price by 11.6% from 43,000 won to 48,000 won. The analysis pointed to three key drivers: a significant increase in profits expected next year, the Artificial Intelligence Data Center (AIDC) business, and opportunities to enter large-scale overseas nuclear power plant projects. The potential upside compared to the September 18 closing price (36,850 won) is 30.3%. GS Engineering & Construction Headquarters Building (Grand Seoul) Exterior View KB Securities researcher Jang Moonjoon stated, "If profit growth and the AIDC business provide a floor for the share price, what will raise the ceiling is the potential for the company to enter large-scale overseas nuclear power plant projects." He also selected GS Engineering & Construction as his second-most preferred stock in the sector. GS Engineering & Construction, which earns more than 57.2% of its revenue from architectural and residential construction, is expected to underperform its competitors this year. Although the construction industry as a whole is seeing a distinct recovery in profits as the cost ratio of residential construction (the proportion of construction cost to revenue) stabilizes, GS Engineering & Construction's operating profit is expected to decrease to 396 billion won this year, down from 438 billion won last year, due to various cost-related issues. Accordingly, KB Securities revised down its operating profit forecast for this year by 11.6%. Paradoxically, KB Securities believes that this year's underperformance will make next year's rebound stand out even more. KB Securities forecasts next year's operating profit for GS Engineering & Construction to reach 624.3 billion won, more than 57% higher than this year, and net profit attributable to controlling shareholders to jump from 138 billion won to 346 billion won, an increase of about 2.5 times. Researcher Jang analyzed, "Ironically, as the year-end approaches, the likelihood of profit growth exceeding the sector average next year will come into greater focus." AIDC was cited as a mid- to long-term growth driver. Since the expansion of the domestic housing business remains limited, data centers are expected to become a key factor in driving both revenue and profit. Researcher Jang emphasized, "While most major domestic construction companies are highlighting data centers as a future growth engine, GS Engineering & Construction has a clear competitive edge by being able to secure tangible business opportunities in the short term, such as the Donghae AIDC project." The first gateway for overseas nuclear power plant expansion is Vietnam. Korea Electric Power Corporation, along with Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power and others, is working to win the Ninh Thuan 2 nuclear power plant project in Vietnam, with the main contractor for the 'Team Korea' consortium expected to be selected between late this year and early next year. GS Engineering & Construction is bidding as a participating contractor (not the lead contractor) in hopes of making its first overseas entry into the nuclear power plant sector. © The Asia Business Daily. title: Ryan Serhant on the Art of Selling Luxury Real Estate - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. The luxury real estate brokerage SERHANT. generates over $1 billion in transactions every month. On Talks at GS, Ryan Serhant, founder and CEO of SERHANT., joins Tucker York, chair of Goldman Sachs Wealth Management, to discuss his transition from the theatre to real estate during the 2008 financial crisis, his video-led sales strategies, and how calculated risks have led to the company’s success. This episode was recorded on July 16, 2026. Ryan Serhant: Selling is a transfer of enthusiasm in whatever it is you're selling, but you've got to make a choice every day, "Today is going to be great, and here's why." Tucker York: I think I've got a couple of pages of introduction of you, Ryan, but we've decided that people here kind of know who you are, Ryan Serhant. Welcome to Goldman Sachs. Ryan Serhant: Thanks so much. Thanks for having me. Let's do this. Tucker York: Okay. A lot of people know who you are. Seen the TV. Know about the business. Know about the social media, all that kind of stuff, who you are today. I'm just interested to go back to kind of like, how did you get to this place? So, grew up in the Boston area. Went to Hamilton College. What about the background informs who we have in front of us today? Ryan Serhant: I was always a storyteller. If you ask my parents what my superpower is, they'll say that Ryan could tell stories. And I don't know why, I think it's just a part of my genetics. And so, that kind of morphed into having an interest in theater. My whole family is in finance, but I was always telling stories. And so, when I moved to New York City 20 years ago this month actually in 2006, that's what I wanted to do. And I wanted to do it on stage. Really, really hard to make money. Ran out of money really, really quick. And then I got my real estate license only because I didn't have to go to one spot every day. I didn't want to wait tables or bartend. I didn't really want to go back to school. And I definitely, definitely did not want to move home with my parents. I went home for that Thanksgiving. It was Thanksgiving of 2008. And I was going through my day and some of the rental clients that I was meeting in Bronx and Harlem and everything. And I just remember looking up, and I have three sisters and two brothers, and everyone was just staring at me. I was like, what? And my little brother goes, "Dude, you've changed." I'm like, "What do you mean? I haven't changed." He's like, "You talk so fast now." Like, "I don't talk fast. You talk slow. Maybe you should move to New York. In a New York minute we got deals to do. I got money to make. Let's go." And so, I think I'm a bit of a product of my environment. You know, New York City is an incredibly intellectually curious ecosystem. And it enables you to shoot for the stars. But it will also provide you the opportunity to bury yourself in the pavement. And I think it gives you the tools to work as hard as you possibly can to build as much as you can. So, to answer your question, I don't think I thought about it that much. I knew theater is what I liked. I liked performing. I liked being in front of the camera. I liked being on stage. And I just hustled and did auditions all day long. I got into a soap opera. Then they killed me. I was a pretty famous hand model for a while. Ryan Serhant: I'm dually talented, man. I was born with two of these babies. I'm very thankful. And so, that paid the rent a little bit. And then it just got to the point where I needed to figure out what to do with my life. I wanted to be successful, and I knew what it was like to be in New York City and not have money. And I never wanted to go back there. Tucker York: When I think about where you've ultimately had huge success on the real estate side, this is a tough business that requires a huge amount of perseverance, rejection, all that. Similar to what you hear about all the acting stories. I came to New York. I didn't get the role, but I kept going, I kept going, I kept going. And it sounds the way you talk about it, it was less about, I wanted to be necessarily an actor. I wanted to have enough money to be able to do something I wanted to do. Ryan Serhant: Yeah, it was-- My dad always told me, "You can quit whenever you want at anything you do, but you're only allowed to quit on your best day." And I've never forgotten that. At the end of the day, you have to do an internal check-in where you tell yourself, was today a day a bad day, a good day, or a great day. And if you don't do that, you're going to blink, and 10 years are going to go by. Right? 15 years are going to go by. And you're going to wake up in a life that you worked really, really hard to get to, that you actually resent. And that can happen really quickly, especially in New York. And so, I made very sure that I say, ready, set, go. And at the end of every day, I know where I am. And so, yeah, you quit on your best day. Tucker York: It's a good call. I'm going to get to, like, the really, really good days that follow this. But 2008 is the time when you decide this acting thing's kind of hard. It's not really going to work. I need to make some money. Kind of like, let's sell real estate at the beginning of the global financial crisis. Ryan Serhant: Yeah. It wasn't really-- I mean, yes. Looking back on it, absolute worst time possible to get into the real estate business. For me, like, I had no money. So, it was summer of 2008. I didn't know what else to do. And so, a friend said, "Get your real estate license. Meet people on Craigslist. And then you'll figure it out." All I had to do was make $2,000 a month, and I didn't have to move home. The day I got my license and started, it just so happened to be the day Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy. And to me, you know, I just thought everyone just loses their job all the time. Like, man, every client I would get. Then they would get fired a month later. And then they couldn't close, and you couldn't get a mortgage. But in retrospect, what ended up happening, because so many people got out of the business, and because I was so ignorant, and ignorance in motion wins all the time over intelligence at rest, I just moved as fast as I could. 82% of all newly licensed agents in the United States quit in the first two years. They try it and they bail because it's too hard. There's no salary. There are no benefits. You eat what you kill. Buyers are liars. And sellers will also lie to you, right? Tucker York: Again, these are the four years before you're on TV. And the reality is, you're, like, incredible. Incredibly focused, all in, cold calling. Doing all that kind of stuff all the time. Is that what made you successful? Ryan Serhant: Not at the beginning. The acting business teaches you the art of rejection. And you have to be able to take 52 punches right in the nose and say, "Thank you, sir, may I have another?" Otherwise, you can't do the bit. You have to move home. But you learn that even though people say, "I don't like you because of your face," you have to keep moving. And for me, the rejection on an apartment was never because of my hair. In fact, my hair was super helpful. Because I have an old man set of hair, but a young boy face, and especially at that time, I would meet clients, and they would look at me, and then they would look up, and they'd say, "How long have you been in this business?" Instead of saying how old are you. And I would just say, "A while." And "a while" is great marketing. So, I did a couple things. One was Craigslist ads. And I would just meet people cold. And I would post ads for apartments and have keys in my pocket and run around. Two was I would just go on the street. The best part about New York was that every single person outside was a potential client. And so, I would stand outside Saks Fifth Avenue because our office was at 20 East 49th. If you had more than two shopping bags, you could probably afford a new apartment. I had business cards back then, old school business cards, and I would say, you know, "My name is Ryan Serhant. If you're looking to buy or sell or rent in New York City, please reach out to me." Some of those people and their families are still clients to this day. Tucker York: You do the hard work during this period of time. And then you catch this gig on TV. Ryan Serhant: Luck is what happens when opportunity meets hard work. And hard work trumps luck when luck doesn't work hard. And so, I'd spent my entire life thinking I was going to do X. And it didn't work out for me. And instead of treating it like a brick wall, which a lot of people do, I treat every obstacle like a speed bump. In the grand scheme of life, it's just a speed bump. Just keep driving. That's what I did when theater didn't work out and got into real estate. I put theater to the side. I put acting to the side. And then there was an open casting call in Times Square for Million Dollar Listing in New York in March of 2010. And I went just because why not? Why would I not go? And I'd done stuff, you know, on camera before. And 3,000 real estate agents showed up. And then they whittled us down over the course of nine months to four of us. They shot the first season of that show with all four of us. And they told us, at the beginning, "Only three of you will make the final cut. So, be good." And so, I just did what I've always done. I just buckled down, and I just grinded, and I knew the one thing that I had was a relentless sense of optimism. Even in our company today, optimism is not a personality trait. It is an operational discipline. Everything can be bad for everybody all the time. There are always ups. There are always downs. But you've got to make a choice every day, today is going to be great, and here's why. And then the show happened, and, you know, ran for 10 years. Tucker York: So, by the way, the optimism thing, too, it's infectious. Ryan Serhant: Selling is a transfer of enthusiasm in whatever it is you're selling. Tucker York: So, you're on TV. The TV helps the real estate, helps the TV, right? Tucker York: Things are going legitimately great for you until we get to the next global crisis, COVID, and you decide, hey, let's end this and start a company. What's the motivation? Is it greed? Is it fear? Ryan Serhant: By 2018, I had the number one residential selling real estate team in New York City history. I had four television shows. I was writing my first book. I had all this stuff that I was doing, and I didn't know what was next. Am I just going to sell real estate? And also, I saw that the world was starting to change. I saw that real estate was moving from being something that was searchable to something that was discoverable. I have never used my company for distribution ever, because in Instagram and in YouTube, where we started doing property tours and promoting real estate at a social level in 2013 and 2014, I could generate more qualified eyeballs for a singular property in ten minutes than any other firm could ever pay for combined. And most people start businesses, I think, completely backwards. They say, "I want to make a profit. How do I make profit? I'm going to create a product. Great. How do I do that? I need people. Okay, why are people going to work for me?" And for me, I did it literally the exact opposite. I have a clear purpose. I'm going to align that with the right people. If you believe in what I'm doing, great. If you don't, you don't have to work for me. We can then sell any product to make all the profit. Tucker York: So, but tell us. Describe SERHANT beyond, if you will. Just the real estate brokerage that it is, but it's other things. Ryan Serhant: Yeah, we have four key businesses. One is the brokerage, which predominantly operates in the cloud. We operate in 17 states. We'll operate in about 25 states by the end of the year. You know, we do about right now just over a billion dollars a month in transactions. We then have Sellit.com, which is our education business. We have Studios, which is our in-house production studio, which is our top of funnel lead generator. So, we create more content for real estate than any other firm on earth combined per month, and we use that to generate organic lead flow. So, our customer acquisition cost is zero. Tucker York: Just because we talked about this before, compare that to other people's customer acquisition cost. Ryan Serhant: You buy them. I mean, you have to buy revenue. Tucker York: The model is to spend millions of dollars advertising stuff, right? Ryan Serhant: Yeah. You advertise to buy customers. And for real estate agents, right, you have to buy them as well. You have to incentivize them to come to you. We buy zero people. We've never bought a single real estate agent ever. People leave tons and tons of money on the table at other firms, and they come to us, and they win with us. I think that's why our agents are the best of the best in the markets that we're in. One of the reasons I also was excited to be asked to be here today, too, is I use the Goldman analogy a lot, right? My interest is not in being the biggest. It is just in being the best. And if I can provide the absolute best service with the best people to the best clients, you can create a pretty great and differentiated company that way. And then they're S.MPLE. S.MPLE is, think of it as, you know, Uber for the home transaction. So, we have technology that empowers the driver who are agents. My goal is to build a transaction platform that is consumer-facing that grabs that $400 trillion total addressable market, right? In the only AI vertical way that you've ever been able to create. I mean, the technology that we have today will solve the greatest problem I've ever had as a real estate agent, which is, how do I take 129 steps and put it in one thing to get a home sold? And you just could never do it until, like, nine months ago. Tucker York: People-intensive business, relationships will still matter, I assume. Ryan Serhant: Yes. Yeah, it doesn't replace trust. I sold a house, a series of houses, last year for $308 million. The most expensive residential transaction in all of 2025 in the United States to somebody very much in the AI space. And he was very, very interested in sales as a skill set that is irreplaceably human. Tucker York: He was studying your Jedi mind tricks. Ryan Serhant: Yeah, my goal with AI, and I think everyone's goal, is how do you superpower human skill so that you can do what you do best and you can actually have more time to build those relationships and build that trust with your clients. Tucker York: Comments about the real estate market today. I find that real estate people say, "Oh, this is the best time to buy and it's the best time to sell," right? Ryan Serhant: Always. Everyone's business is great until it's not. And so, when it rains, grab your buckets. And we are definitely in a bifurcated housing market. And I hardly ever actually use the phrase "housing market" because I really do think we have a housing obstacle course in this country with how difficult and kind of friction the process is. But you have people who can pay cash and you have everybody else. And it used to have parity. Because you have people who would pay cash because they could, but then it was easy and relatively inexpensive to get a mortgage. For the past four years, it has not been so. Inventory is at all-time-lows, year after year after year. But you're starting to see some of that wake up. People have life changes and they adjust to a new normal, which is happening now. Transaction volume is high. The super luxury market is incredibly high. There are massive transactions that are happening all over the country. The first-time home buyer market is incredibly well funded by their parents. So, they've been doing a great job as well. And we continue to move forward. You know, we don't have a housing crisis. We have a housing supply issue. We just have to create more supply. We have to create tax credits. We do commercial now at our company, which is really interesting. So, you're starting to see municipalities start to release kind of derelict office buildings, space they don't have, which is great for the repurpose into residential space. And so, we're doing a lot of that too, to try to do our part to solve the problem. Tucker York: So, we're a large company, we've been around for a long time. And there's a big mentorship culture here and people that have been around here for a long time. Tucker York: And the people that have been around here for a long time also knew it was like when they came in. And so, it's a pay it forward kind of thing. You didn't really have that experience. You're kind of self-taught. Who are the people that kind of help you? How do you get that input? Ryan Serhant: When I started, I had none at all. Everyone told me not to get into real estate. Everyone told me not to do Million Dollar Listing. Everyone for sure told me not to start my own company. And I went the exact opposite way. I have a lot of great clients, incredibly successful clients, that I can call at any time and ask them for advice. But also, I'm only ever going to catch myself. Like I've got to stare at myself in the mirror every day. And so, I'm the one who's going to take the risk. And if things go well, it's because of everybody else. And if things go poorly, it's 100% my fault. And that's the deal I made with myself when I came to New York City. And that's the deal I made with myself when we started the company. You know, my ambition when I first came to the city was, let me figure this out. I've got to try it. I'd rather regret the things I did than the things I never tried. Let's move. Today, I think people confuse my ambition with responsibility. Because if you knew how many other people really win when I win, you'd understand that it's not for Ryan. It's for everybody else. I surround myself with people far smarter than me every single day. I hire intrapreneurs. So, the same way if you're ever building a team or anyone here who's hiring, you want to hire people that, one, make you a little bit afraid because they're so good and they're going to take your job. Otherwise, why work with them? And two, that you're going to be able to really, really, you know, learn from. Tucker York: What's the advice? What's the kind of the learnings in the last 20 years, what you've done, everything else you would share with people, sort of more broadly as they think about career? Ryan Serhant: My go-to is always to take care of the work. And if you take care of the work, the work will take care of you. I meet a lot of people who are very, very outcome focused, which I think is okay. It's good. But really just focusing on, like, well, I've got to get to here and here and here and here, you lose sight of why you're doing the work in the first place. And I think just doing really, really great work day in and day out, if you do that, you will be as successful as you want to be. As long as you move quickly. Speed to lead is a real thing, especially today. As well as taking calculated risks with yourself, with your career. Like, what's the worst that can happen is something that I'll always try to ask myself too. I don't know if that's great advice. But life finds a way. Tucker York: That's your point. Is if you keep working, the odds of that happening are greatly reduced, right? Ryan Serhant: I remember when I first got into real estate and I was running around, I had holes in my shoes, I was exhausted, I was sweaty all the time. And I remember my parents came and visited me in my apartment. And I was complaining about how early I have to wake up, and I'm tired, and this, that, the other. And I remember my dad saying to me, "Do you think that I wanted to go to work every day?" And that sentence, like, blew my mind, you know? Because I grew up with him at State Street in 1993. Like, of course he wanted to go to work. Like, that's what he does. He was Mr. Finance, you know? And so, I knew in that moment, like, okay, I will not complain ever again, and I will just take care of the work, and I will just continue to move forward. Tucker York: Thank you very much for coming to Goldman Sachs and, frankly, sharing a story that I know we all find pretty inspirational and pretty cool. Tucker York: Very successful. Thank you everybody. title: Unveiling Microbial Communities And Biogeochemical Cycles In Antarctic Colored Snow - astrobiology.com
content:
[BMC Microbiology].   Snow cover, the extensive terrestrial habitat in Antarctica, sometimes exhibits vivid coloration, yet the structure and function of its microbial communities remain poorly characterized. Using metagenomic sequencing of red snow (RS) and green snow (GS) from the Fildes Peninsula, we found that bacterial, eukaryotic, and archaeal relative abundances were 85.82%, 13.52% and 0.16%, respectively. β-Diversity differed significantly between RS and GS across these three domains (P < 0.05). Dominant bacterial phyla included Bacteroidota (RS: 62.61%; GS: 38.72%) and Pseudomonadota (RS: 32.80%; GS: 54.10%). Among eukaryotes, Chlorophyta (RS: 58.10%; GS: 52.98%) and Basidiomycota (RS: 14.80%; GS: 8.08%) were prevalent. Nanobdellota dominated archaea, with lower abundance in RS than GS. In the algal community, Sanguina, Gonium and Chloromonas were significantly enriched in red snow, while Chlorella and Micractinium were enriched in green snow (P < 0.05). Marker genes associated with carbon (C), nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and sulfur (S) cycles were identified in green and red snow. Aerobic respiration and phosphate regulation were significantly enriched in red snow, while CO oxidation, fermentation, and denitrification were significantly enriched in green snow. Key microbial genera associated with these functional pathways also varied. In the denitrification of red snow, Stutzerimonas was the most abundant genus, while Janthinobacterium was abundant in green snow. Nitrification-related genes were detected only in red snow based on the present metagenomic data. The network of the red snow microbial community was potentially more complex and resistant based on topology, which not only benefited its own long-term survival but might also have potentially influenced the positive feedback effect of snowmelt by maintaining a low-albedo snow surface. This provided an ecological implication under climate warming: the expansion of red snow patches showed the potential to the increase nitrate runoff export, which would affect nitrogen nutrient levels in coastal Antarctic waters. Overall, this study used metagenomics to compare the multidomain (bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes) composition and diversity between red snow and green snow, and directly linked key microbial taxa with functional genes of biogeochemical cycles. This study provided new insights into the biological characteristics and functional potential of Antarctic colored snow.               send an e-mail Colțești, Romania. After six days of riding, around
  1,500 kilometres and an exceptionally demanding route through the

  Thomann) won the men’s competition with 203 points, while Team Europe
  (Chrissie Harcourt, Anja Filak) prevailed in the women’s competition
  with 200 points. The anniversary edition went farther, higher and was
  more technical than ever before – across narrow forest trails,
  washed-out mountain paths, riverbeds and historic high-altitude
  routes. At the same time, it remained true to what defines the GS
  Trophy: a shared adventure in which team spirit, precision, endurance
  and mutual support matter more than outright speed. The outcome was decided only in the final challenge. Ahead of the
  last day, just two points separated Team International and Team Europe
  in the women’s competition, while Team Germany defended an
  eleven-point lead over Team Europe in the men’s competition. Under
  maximum pressure, the eventual winners demonstrated precisely the
  qualities that defined this GS Trophy: trust, composure and consistent teamwork. In the women’s final, Chrissie Harcourt from Great Britain and
  Anja Filak from the Netherlands rode with control and close
  coordination to secure victory for Team Europe. Team Germany,
  comprising Fabian Fenner, Norman Pleissner and Florian Thomann,
  crowned a consistently strong performance throughout the week with
  overall victory in the men’s competition. BMW Motorrad International GS Trophy 2026 Romania – Final standings.

Women’s teams:
1. Europe – 200 points2. International – 1843.
  Australia – 1644. China – 1595. Germany – 146 Men’s teams:
1. Germany – 203 points2. Europe – 1473. Ukraine –
  1444. Australia – 1385. Japan – 1356. Korea –
  1317. International – 1288. China – 102 The winners of the women’s competition, Team Europe, had not known
  each other before this event: one came from Wales in the United
  Kingdom, the other from the Netherlands. Over the course of the event,
  they grew together as a team and, with mutual support, overcame every
  obstacle on their way to victory. Chrissie Harcourt, Team Europe: “I can hardly
  describe this feeling. My head is a little all over the place;
  everything feels a bit shaky. It will take a while for it to truly
  sink in. I am incredibly proud of both of us.” Anja Filak, Team Europe: “We were certainly the
  smallest team in the competition. But we rode like one body, as one
  unit. Chrissie is amazing. She gave me a lot of advice, and I was able
  to follow her and make it through. I gained more confidence because I
  knew I could follow her and stay focused. I took everything she told
  me over these days very much to heart and tried to put every piece of
  advice into practice – and it worked!” The tenth edition set new benchmarks: six days, around 1,500
  kilometres and approximately half of the route away from paved roads.
  For three consecutive days, the teams spent eleven to twelve hours on
  the move; day three featured more than 300 kilometres, including 170
  kilometres of trails. Cold temperatures, dense fog, wet camps and
  constantly changing terrain made recovery and personal organisation
  just as important as riding skill. The most formidable challenges awaited high in the Carpathians: the
  eight-kilometre Metzeler Enduro Navigation Challenge on narrow single
  trails, the uncompromising climbs to the Strategica Mountain Road and
  an exposed descent along a narrow goat track. Riverbeds, deep fine
  gravel, wet grassy slopes and washed-out forest tracks added to the
  challenge. The combination of distance, technical difficulty,
  navigation and fatigue made Romania one of the toughest and, at the
  same time, most impressive GS Trophies to date. Another defining feature was the interplay between authentic
  adventure and international community. Under the motto “Back to
  Basics”, 30 riders from 13 nations experienced Romania’s wild
  landscapes, historic high-altitude routes and warm hospitality. The

title: RBI sells Rs 25,000 cr govt securities in second OMO tranche to drain surplus liquidity - PSU Watch
content: Mumbai: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Monday accepted bids worth Rs 25,000 crore in the second tranche of its open market operation (OMO) sale of government securities, as it stepped up efforts to absorb surplus liquidity from the banking system. The RBI accepted Rs 11,512 crore of the 6.10 per cent GS 2031, Rs 8,758 crore of the 7.95 per cent GS 2032, Rs 2,300 crore of the 6.75 per cent GS 2029, Rs 2,250 crore of the 7.17 per cent GS 2030, and Rs 180 crore of the 7.17 per cent GS 2028, according to the release. However, the Central bank did not accept any bids for the 8.28 per cent GS 2027, the release said. The OMO sale comes amid a large liquidity surplus in the banking system. Liquidity surplus was estimated around Rs 6.05 lakh crore as of September 20, according to the RBI data. Under an OMO sale, banks and other investors pay the RBI for the government securities, thereby draining rupee liquidity from the banking system. The central bank had announced OMO sales totalling Rs 1 lakh crore in three tranches to manage the prevailing liquidity conditions. The remaining last tranches of Rs 25,000 crore is scheduled for September 28. The banking system was flushed with liquidity due to heavy mobilisation of FCNR (B) deposits by banks, as the mobilisation brought foreign currency into the system, while subsequent swaps with the RBI provided rupee liquidity to banks. Besides FCNR(B) inflows, month-end government expenditure, including payments toward salaries and pensions, also added to liquidity in the banking system. title: Six days, 1500 kilometres and a GS Trophy podium for Australia - MCNews
content: From the wide-open spaces of Mongolia in 2018 to the New Zealand adventure of 2020, MCNews has followed the BMW Motorrad International GS Trophy through some spectacular country. Subsequent editions took the event to Albania in 2022 and Namibia in 2024, before Romania’s Carpathian Mountains supplied the setting for the tenth edition in 2026. And Romania made them work for it. Six days, approximately 1500 kilometres, cold mornings, wet camps and a succession of steep climbs and awkward descents culminated in a rain-affected finale, with Australia’s women claiming third overall and the men finishing just outside the podium in fourth. Germany won the men’s competition, while the European pairing of Chrissie Harcourt and Anja Filak took the women’s honours. Both titles remained in play heading into the final day, despite the much larger margins in the completed standings. The terrain gave the event a very different character from its previous outing in Namibia. Narrow forest trails, washed-out tracks, slippery grass and exposed mountain paths tested the competitors aboard BMW’s R 12 G/S, with roughly half the distance covered off-road. Australia finished the women’s competition on 164 points, five clear of China and 18 ahead of Germany. Team Europe topped the standings with 200, followed by Team International on 184. In the men’s competition, Australia’s 138 points left the team six behind third-placed Ukraine and nine behind runner-up Europe. Japan was only three points further back, underlining how closely the positions behind the winning Germans were contested. Germany’s Fabian Fenner, Norman Pleissner and Florian Thomann finished on 203 points, eventually stretching their advantage over Europe to 56. That final margin disguises a much tighter contest during the week: Germany had entered the last day with an 11-point lead. The 2026 theme was “Back to Basics”, reflected in the choice of the R 12 G/S and an event that placed a premium on bike control, navigation and cooperation. Time mattered in the special tests, but so did accuracy, keeping feet on the pegs and working effectively with team-mates. As detailed in our look at the GS Trophy Competition Bike, the R 12 G/S followed the R 1300 GS used in Namibia and the R 1250 GS ridden in Albania. The air/oil-cooled 1170 cc boxer was equipped with 21-inch front and 18-inch rear wheels, off-road protection and the Enduro Package Pro. Romania put that equipment to use. For the first three days, each rider kept the teams moving for 11 to 12 hours, making fatigue, drying gear, and finding time to recover part of the challenge. Any notion of a gentle introduction disappeared on day one. The Welcome Trial took place on an exposed mountain plateau, where wet grass, off-camber slopes and a steep ascent and descent immediately tested balance and line choice. Putting a foot down, stopping or straying outside the marked course attracted penalties, while the clock added another consideration. The challenge was carrying enough momentum without losing control. The route covered 310 kilometres, including around 150 kilometres of unsealed mountain and forest tracks. The Akrapovič Riverbed Challenge added embankments, soft river deposits and fine gravel to the mix. By late afternoon, there were still 120 kilometres to go, around half of them on technical tracks. The teams finally reached Sighișoara shortly after 6.30 pm, almost 12 hours after setting out. The next morning began at 6°C in dense fog, followed by more than 11 hours of riding through forest sections littered with sand, mud, tight hairpins and deep ruts. Three consecutive climbs provided one of the day’s sternest examinations. The reward at the top was a view across the Carpathians towards the 22.5-metre Sacred Heart of Jesus statue. Help keep independent motorcycle journalism alive Near Valea Zălanului, the route mixed flowing forest tracks with river crossings and alternating stretches of gravel and grass across the floodplain. Riders repeatedly had to adjust to different surfaces and grip levels. Day three delivered another cold, foggy start and another itinerary exceeding 300 kilometres, around 170 of them off-road. Damp kit and limited recovery time were becoming familiar companions. The route climbed into the Tătaru Mountains and onto the high pastures of Tabla Buții, a historic ridge route that once marked a national border and later saw fighting during the First World War. The key riding test was the eight-kilometre Metzeler Enduro Navigation Challenge near Zărnești. Following a GPS track through the forest sounds straightforward enough, until narrow single trails, easily missed junctions and steep embankments are added to the equation. With fatigue accumulating, this ranked among the most technical sections of the entire event. Bran Castle, associated with the Dracula legend, provided a memorable landmark towards the end of the day. After three very long days, a 180-kilometre itinerary offered some relief on paper. The riding still demanded plenty. Sleep had already been interrupted by the guard dogs of nearby shepherds, which kept potential wildlife away from the campsite. A trial on a wet, steeply sloping grass field then ensured everyone was properly awake. The route initially flowed towards the Transfăgărășan before two difficult off-road climbs raised the workload again. One demanded precise positioning within a confined space; the other followed a deeply rutted double track along the mountainside, where maintaining traction was critical. The Lotru Riding Challenge finished the competitive programme with a comparatively fast run through rock fields and deep fine gravel in the riverbed. By 4.30 pm the test was complete, finally leaving a little more time for recovery and catching up with the other teams. The fifth day covered more than 300 kilometres back to base camp in Colțești, with the Strategica Mountain Road at its centre. Built as a military road during the First World War, the high-altitude route combined spectacular scenery with steep, technical climbs. Failed attempts could require difficult recoveries, and reaching the top did not signal the end of the hard work. The descent followed a narrow, exposed mountain trail that demanded absolute concentration. Further climbs and steep descents eventually brought the riders to the winding Transalpina, providing a spell on asphalt before more tracks led back towards camp. The final morning began with a 120-kilometre loop, evenly divided between sealed roads and unpaved tracks along mountain ridges. Heavier rain then interrupted proceedings, leaving increasingly wet ground for the climbs leading to the last special test. Its two-part layout began with a faster passage across off-camber grass before tightening into a technical section of steep embankments and rock steps. Only two points had separated Team International and Team Europe in the women’s standings before the final day. Harcourt, from Great Britain, and Filak, from the Netherlands, delivered under pressure to secure the title for Europe. The pair had not known each other before the event, making their ability to develop an effective partnership over the six days a particularly fitting GS Trophy success story. “I can hardly describe this feeling. My head is a little all over the place; everything feels a bit shaky. It will take a while for it to truly sink in. I am incredibly proud of both of us.” “We were certainly the smallest team in the competition. But we rode like one body, as one unit. Chrissie is amazing. She gave me a lot of advice, and I was able to follow her and make it through. I gained more confidence because I knew I could follow her and stay focused. I took everything she told me over these days very much to heart and tried to put every piece of advice into practice – and it worked!” Germany also completed the job in the men’s competition, with Fenner, Pleissner and Thomann converting their overnight advantage into the overall win. GS Trophy marshal Matei Albulescu played a central role in bringing the event to his home country, helping scout the route and working with landowners and authorities to secure access. Tabla Buții and Strategica were among his personal favourites, and they helped give the anniversary edition its distinctive mix of history, remote terrain and demanding riding. Even the scoring stayed deliberately simple: marshals assessed the specials with pen and paper, calculated results by hand, and updated the leaderboard each evening. Those numbers ultimately put Germany and Europe on top. For Australia, a women’s podium and fourth in the men’s standings capped six demanding days in a host country that gave the GS Trophy’s tenth edition plenty to remember. title: GS holds 5th hackathon as chairman says AI is transforming workplace safety - mbiz.heraldcorp.com
content: GS Group held its 5th GS Group Hackathon on Monday at the Westin Seoul Parnas in Gangnam-gu, Seoul. The hackathon brings together GS employees to propose ideas using AI, from in-house productivity improvements to broader business innovations. A total of 923 people are expected to participate through Tuesday — 797 employees from GS affiliates and 126 external participants — making it the largest edition to date. Cumulative participation over the past five years has reached 2,732. This year's theme is "Play with Gen AI Season 3: Build and Act," reflecting a dual focus on creating AI-powered outputs that actually work (Build) and connecting them to real workplaces and business operations (Act). GS Group Chairman Heo Tae-soo, who attended the event, said ideas from employees who know the workplace best, combined with AI, had become a force for changing how industrial safety is managed. "I will actively support the challenges that began at the hackathon so they can take root beyond GS, reach more workplaces and lead to new value," he said. GS Caltex Vice Chairman and CEO Heo Se-hong, who delivered the opening remarks, said the hackathon was a place to bring out and act on ideas that are rarely tried in everyday work. "I hope you spend the next two days asking questions freely, taking on challenges and discovering new possibilities," he said. This year's participants are working with AI-ready data. Applying AI to industrial settings requires data to be organized in a format that AI can read — a step that must come first. Even when data has accumulated on-site, inconsistent formats and standards make retrieving and processing it time-consuming. To ease this bottleneck, GS has been refining and structuring data gathered across various business sites, including power plants and convenience stores. Its innovation unit 52g, for example, has organized tacit knowledge from GS Donghae Power — covering operations, maintenance and facilities — into AI-readable form, and is developing a power-plant-specific AI model that understands on-site knowledge and work procedures. At this hackathon, participants are combining AI-ready data with GS's AI transformation platform MISO to solve real workplace problems. The key is cutting the time spent on data preparation so ideas can be implemented faster and deployed on-site sooner. Kim Jin-a, a GS executive director who helped organize the hackathon, said five years of the event had established GS's field-centered AI transformation as an innovation model that drives real change, beyond slogans or one-off experiments. "We plan to support this year's outputs through verification and refinement so they translate into tangible results in actual work and business performance," she said. Meanwhile, the safety management AI agent team AIR (AI Risk Assessment) received the Open Innovation Award at the event. AIR originated from an idea proposed at the 3rd GS Group Hackathon by five employees from GS Power's safety and mechanical divisions. Users enter a task name and a brief description, and the AI automatically identifies potential hazards, assigns risk ratings and suggests preventive safety measures. Built by frontline workers rather than professional developers using MISO, it is now in use at more than 330 worksites, including small and midsize businesses.

title: GS Chairman Pledges Support for AI Innovation at Work Sites - Seoul Economic Daily

Chairman Huh Visits Venue and Presents Award GS Group Chairman Huh Tae-soo visited the group's hackathon in person to encourage its artificial intelligence achievements and press for an AI transition rooted in actual industrial work sites. GS Group said the 5th GS Group Hackathon will run for two days from the 21st at the Grand InterContinental Seoul Parnas in Seoul's Gangnam district. A total of 923 people are taking part — 797 employees from GS affiliates and 126 outside participants — making it the largest event of its kind to date. The title reflects a shift beyond proposing ideas toward building working products with AI and connecting them to day-to-day operations and business sites. Participants combined "AI Ready data," refined and structured by GS from work sites such as power plants and convenience stores, with MISO, the group's in-house AI transformation platform, to carry out practical field assignments. Huh, who attended the event that day, personally presented the Open Innovation Award to the team behind AIR, an AI agent for safety management. AIR grew out of an idea proposed by GS Power employees at the third hackathon. When a user enters details of a task, the AI provides a risk rating and preventive measures in real time. The system has since been rolled out to about 330 work sites, including those at small and midsize companies. "Ideas from the people who know the work sites best met AI and became a force that changed how safety is managed on site," Huh said. "We will actively support this effort so that the challenge takes root at more industrial work sites beyond GS and leads to new value." "Push ahead as much as you like and discover new possibilities." The venue also featured booths from global technology companies including Amazon Web Services and OpenAI, along with space for demonstrations of robotics-integrated technology from companies such as AgiBot. The GS Group Hackathon began in 2022 as an event for solving problems with digital technology and, from 2024, shifted in earnest to generative AI use centered on MISO. title: Mailbag: Fans React After Vikings Hold Bears Scoreless on 9 Consecutive Possessions in 9-3 Win - Minnesota Vikings
content:
Do you have a comment or question? Send it to the Mailbag. Every Monday we'll post several comments and/or questions. Click here to submit a comment or question to Mailbag. Remember to include your name and town in the email. If Twitter / X is your jam, you can send a question to me that way as well. The Vikings have started 2-0 with both wins coming against division foes for the first time since 2003 and third time ever. Minnesota's defense bowed up at the critical moments, denying Chicago points on all but one drive (the first of the game for the Bears) and held on for a 9-3 win in the lowest-scoring game in series history. The Bears put together a 13-play drive that gained 51 yards before a string of penalties forced a punt. An 11-play, 64-yarder to open the second half ended when Jalen Redmond forced a fumble recovered by Isaiah Rodgers at the Minnesota 1. A 12-play, 62-yarder ended with Rodgers blocking a 23-yard field goal, and an eight-play drive covered 44 yards but ended at the Minnesota 12 on the game's final snap, which was hiked with one second remaining. The offense leaned on getting points on the opening drive by taking an early chance — a 30-yard pass from Carson Wentz to Justin Jefferson that moved the receiver past Randy Moss for second on Minnesota's all-time catches leaderboard — and leaned on the reliability and ruggedness of Aaron Jones, Sr., who improved to 16-2 in 18 career games against the Bears. Will Reichard was good on field goals of 35, 49 and 39 yards, despite some soggy socks and shoes. View game action photos from the Vikings Week 2 game vs. the Bears at Soldier Field. What a great defensive battle this game was. The ending was just insane. So sorry to see Caleb Williams go down on that non-contact injury. I was just amazed at the fourth quarter blocked FG and subsequent drive — earning a rare fourth up! Below are my four ups and three downs for the game: 1. Vikings defense forcing Caleb to make a poor first quarter throw on third-and-long resulting in a Vikings interception. Nicely done! 2. Outstanding defensive play heading into the end of the half. We forced a punt and after our offense stalled and we punted, we stopped their final drive as well. 3. Redmond's punch-out fumble by the Vikings defense on the Bears 1-yard line.  Excellent play. 4. The fourth quarter blocked FG and, just as important, the almost game-sealing drive where we ran the ball and milked the clock. Only to have the defense save the day with no time on the clock. Wow. 1. Third-and-2 for Vikings. Ends up with play clock running out and snap over Wentz's head. Unacceptable on both fronts. 2. At the end of the half we had to punt. Great punt and weak and ineffective punt coverage when it mattered most. We set the conditions for Caleb to tie the game or take the lead by allowing that return. Our punt coverage team should be thanking our defense for their second 2-minute stop. 3. Overall offensive production was too weak. But I will take that fourth quarter drive any time! I obviously never want any player to go through an injury, regardless of what team he plays for and wish Williams well in his recovery. Injuries are part of the game, and the Vikings have gone through many over the years. Prior to Williams' injury, it seemed like the Vikings designed and executed a great game plan that constrained a team that scored 59 points at Carolina in Week 1. Having covered teams that have fallen victim to the "Peanut Punch" copyrighted by Charles Tillman, it was impressive to see Redmond's wallop with Tillman in attendance. Rodgers grazed Cairo Santos' field goal at the end of Chicago's first possession and brought an even better one on his next try, keeping it a 6-3 game with 6:21 remaining. There seemed to be a bit of disarray prior to the snap. Perhaps a timeout would have been in order. It was super critical that Wentz hustled to recover the ball. Brett Thorson held for all three field goals and punted six times for 297 yards. His 62-yarder was returned 24 yards by Kalif Raymond, so it only netted 38, but Thorson did really well in his second pro game. Ugly win, but a win is a win! 9–3, and that defense was lights out. Offense has a LOT to clean up — good thing we weren't facing an elite defense today. Aaron Jones carried the load, and our defense slammed the door. SKOL! 😈🔥 We'll have more on the defense in a bit, but how about Jones? The Vikings were without running back Jordan Mason, as well as receiver Jauan Jennings but stayed committed to the run game. Jones shouldered 23 of the team's 28 rush attempts, going 12 for 52 yards in the first half and 11 for 53 in the second half. He withstood needing to come off the field after a facemask issue and later lost his helmet during a big hit but remained undeterred. Ugly wins count the same. And bad weather games can produce ugly wins. The numbers and stats don't tell much of a story in this game until you look at turnovers. And turnovers usually tell the win/loss story of most games. In this game. A 2-0 turnover differential in Chicago leads to a 2-0 record for Minnesota. The three phases of the Vikings team win bear (pun intended) analysis. I have been critical of the stated offensive philosophy to feature the run more. I've seen it fail too many times. So far, the balance I have seen in the offense gives me hope. The Flores defense remains a mystery for other teams to solve. And timely special teams play created all Vikings scores and prevented at least one for Chicago. What a FG block! Hated seeing the Caleb Williams injury. But would his presence have made a difference at the end? We won't ever know. We do know the Vikings lead the division, and Will Reichard remains reliable even on doinks. Turnovers are quite often a deciding factor in the outcome of games. Kevin O'Connell improved to 37-4 when the Vikings are even or better in the turnover differential stat. Ball control and minimizing the damage when there was a miscue (the wayward snap) were super important to Minnesota's success in those conditions. Wow, does it feel good to be (not just) 2-0, but 2-0 in the division to start the season. While I don't think anyone would call these wins pretty, they have been gritty! Respect to the run game this week. We finally saw ourselves running the ball to where we had numerous third-and-less-than-5 situations, something this team has struggled to achieve the past couple seasons. The question mark came as we had similar results converting those third downs as we've had with third-and-long. Credit to the defenses of course, but third-down conversions still seem like a difficult task for our team compared to others. Dallas Turner is the real deal and starting to show out in ways reminiscent of Danielle Hunter! Isaiah Rodgers another huge performance. Great effort by that defense to control the game and confound the offense. Any chance for the fans health we can eliminate the game terror of giving up big drives to the opponent in the last minute of each half? The third-down percentage (Minnesota went 3-for-13) definitely has room for improvement, but there were some clutch plays at different points of the game. Turner's power on the game-sealing sack was impressive. The play calls and philosophy changes at the end of halves, but that also is the one spot where the defense could have tried to close the door a little earlier. Ideally the offense would have gotten one more first down to finish in victory. But, I guess will take another highlight going on Turner's resume tape. Which makes me wonder: what would have happened if Brian Flores was coaching the Vikings defense in the 1970s instead of today? Can you imagine if he had masterminded the Purple People Eaters? Is it possible that they would have been even better? I'm not sure that any of the offenses of the '70s would have had an answer for his defensive schemes. The EWIND is available for viewing and test drives at the GS Evo Motors showroom. It comes with an eight-year or 150,000-km battery warranty and a five-year or 150,000-km vehicle warranty. Australian High Commissioner to Sri Lanka Matthew Duckworth described Omega Traders’ latest investment in a modern dhal-processing facility as a strong example of how cross-border supply chains can translate into productive investment, local value addition and new business opportunities in Sri Lanka. The investment, which adds a 150-metric-tonne-per-eight-hour-day processing capacity to Omega Traders’ operations, marks a significant expansion of the company’s manufacturing footprint as it celebrates 45 years in Sri Lanka’s food commodity industry. Speaking at the inauguration of the new Lentil and Orid Dhal Processing Factory in Wattala, last Friday, H.C. Duckworth said the facility represented more than an increase in production capacity, pointing to the wider economic value created when Australian agricultural production is connected with Sri Lankan processing and distribution. ‘This facility is not operating on its own. It is part of a long supply chain and a trade partnership between Sri Lanka and Australia, Duckworth said. His comments placed the Omega Traders’ investment within a broader commercial context: Australia brings agricultural production and established export capabilities, while Sri Lanka provides processing capacity, labour, market access and opportunities for further value addition. The investment comes as Sri Lanka continues to look towards greater domestic processing and value-added manufacturing rather than relying solely on the import and distribution of finished commodities. Dr. (Mrs.) Siddhika G. Senaratne, Director General/CEO of the Sri Lanka Standards Institution (SLSI), who attended the inauguration as Guest of Honour, highlighted the importance of quality assurance in food processing and the role of standards in maintaining confidence across the supply chain. The facility is equipped with new-generation cleaning, processing, sorting and quality-control machinery, including advanced colour-sorting technology, automated systems and an in-house quality-control laboratory. The additional capacity will support Omega Traders’ three principal Mysoor Dhal brands — Rainbow Jumbo Dhal, Komas Dhal and Rozanna Dhal — which serve different segments of the Sri Lankan market. But the investment also has a distinctly local agricultural dimension. Through its Orid Dhal operation, Omega Traders plans to source locally grown black matpe from Sri Lankan farmers and process it at the new facility. That creates a domestic value chain linking farmers to industrial processing and consumers, while potentially increasing demand for locally produced agricultural commodities. Duckworth said this type of business partnership could generate benefits for both countries. ‘Australia produces some of the world’s best agricultural products and we are very efficient and very capable at trading them. But that alone is not going to bring success to Australia. Just as building a factory like this is not going to bring success to Sri Lanka, he said. ‘It’s when we bring these entities together that our products produced in Australia can be processed in excellence here in Sri Lanka that enables this to be a success, the H.C. explained. The investment therefore combines two complementary supply streams: imported agricultural commodities, including Australian-origin products, and locally produced black matpe for the Orid Dhal operation. For Sri Lanka, the business significance extends beyond Omega Traders itself. Increased processing capacity creates demand for logistics, packaging, distribution, services and agricultural inputs, while supporting employment within the food-processing ecosystem. title: GS Engineering & Construction holds AI competition finals, eyes real-world deployment - mbiz.heraldcorp.com
content: Over 90 teams competed; 700-plus employees trained and coached Top prize goes to AI solution for reviewing plant steel shop drawings GS Engineering & Construction is accelerating its digital transformation by moving beyond company-wide AI training to deploying employee-developed AI solutions in actual construction work. The company announced Monday that it had selected 12 projects with strong real-world applicability through its in-house AI competition, AX Recipe, and held the finals Friday. At the finals, 12 teams demonstrated AI solutions they had developed themselves. Voting by management, including CEO Heo Yun-hong, and employees determined the top three teams. This year's top prize went to an AI solution for streamlining the review of plant steel shop drawings. The winning entry replaced a manual process of visually cross-checking thousands of steel members one by one with an AI-based solution, cutting review time by more than 80 percent and significantly improving accuracy. The representative of the winning team will receive an invitation to attend CES 2027, the world's largest consumer electronics and IT trade show. Now in its second year, AX Recipe — launched last year — is GS Engineering & Construction's flagship innovation program in which employees use AI to solve real workplace problems. This year the format shifted from individual to team participation, yielding a broad range of practical AI solutions ready for immediate deployment across the company's business lines, including architecture, infrastructure and plant construction, going well beyond simple task automation. More than 90 teams entered the competition, and some 700 employees received AI training and dedicated coaching over July and August. The finals showcased a variety of construction-specific ideas, including a defect-prevention platform integration solution for the design and construction phases, a project contract change tracking system, and a solution for cross-checking 3D design models against specifications. GS Engineering & Construction plans to review the top projects for broader rollout across divisions and the company before applying them to operations in stages. "Through AX Recipe, we confirmed that our employees can go beyond learning about AI to actually applying it on the job and delivering tangible results," a company official said. "We will continue to strengthen a system that organically connects training, hands-on practice and real-world application, and we will keep expanding a data and AI utilization model tailored to the construction industry." Meanwhile, GS Engineering & Construction posted operating profit of 232.4 billion won ($168 million) in the first half of this year, up 41.8 percent from 164.2 billion won in the same period last year.

title: [INTERVIEW] Authentic Korean convenience meals attract foreigners - The Korea Times
content: Min Jung-hwan of GS Retail says Korean convenience store dosirak are drawing foreigners because they want authentic Korean-style meals. GS25 is expanding offerings with banchan such as bulgogi, dakgangjeong and japchae, while keeping prices generally under 7,000 won. The company says demand is being driven by lunchflation, better quality and more varied recipes. GS25 also says it launches new dosirak through consumer surveys, testing and a roughly 12-week production process. Min Jung-hwan, a merchandiser with GS Retail’s Fresh Food Team, poses next to the company’s logo at their headquarters in Gangnam District, Seoul, Sept. 7. Courtesy of GS Retail The global popularity of Korean food has reached a point where convenience store meal boxes, known as “dosirak,” have become part of a new market trend where signature Korean flavors and traditional recipes have become a hit with international visitors and popular in new markets. Min Jung-hwan, who plans and oversees dosirak production for GS25 at GS Retail’s Merchandise Headquarters, is seeing the shift firsthand. Rather than creating separate products for foreign customers, the retailer is increasingly offering the same dosirak that appeal to Korean consumers, reflecting growing interest in authentic Korean flavors. “We don’t make dosirak that are specially for foreigners because many of them like what Koreans enjoy. Even at GS25 stores in Vietnam and Mongolia, visitors are interested in authentic Korean-style dosirak. We try to meet such expectations so that they can feel they are inside a Korean convenience store,” Min said in an interview with The Korea Times. “To serve the rising number of foreigners coming to Korea, we are boosting a pipeline for those with banchan (side dishes) they usually like, including bulgogi (marinated meat), dakgangjeong (fried chicken in sauce) or japchae (stir-fried glass noodles with vegetables).” Dosirak have continuously evolved alongside Korea’s convenience store industry, driven by their enduring popularity. The changes go beyond the quality of the food, encompassing a wider variety of banchan, more diverse packaging and a growing focus on the tastes and needs of a diverse group of consumers. Min Jung-hwan poses with a dosirak inside a GS25 store in Seoul, Sept. 7. Inside the store are ready-to-eat fresh food items, including dosirak, gimbap, hamburgers and sandwiches. Courtesy of GS Retail The trend is propelled in part by increased prices across retail and dine-in markets, driving the consumers to seek more affordable foods. For those who have to eat meals while on the run, convenience stores have become an ideal spot to grab a bite, with dosirak and other fresh food items rarely exceeding 7,000 won ($5.21). Min said the trend shows that convenience store foods have evolved beyond their image as cheap, simple meals. “It is true that 'lunchflation' has heightened people’s sensitivity to how much they have to pay, so it has expanded the markets for affordable convenience store dosirak,” Min said. “What’s different now from the past is the level of quality. In the past, dosirak had to be cheap and were merely an alternative to ordinary meals. Now, they have become a popular category. They use seasonal ingredients to introduce eye-catching items like spring cabbage bibimbap. They have gotten more expensive, too, but they are still popular among those who are willing to pay for taste satisfaction. Our most popular dosirak is 6,900 won. In the past, those priced below 6,000 won sold the best.” Marketing efforts have also raised consumers’ expectations. The company has collaborated with Choi Kang-rok, the winner of the second season of Netflix’s “Culinary Class Wars,” on new dosirak. GS25 has also launched a “Dosirak of the Month” program, fueling consumer curiosity and driving sales. "Hyeja Dosirak," featuring actress Kim Hye-ja, has been one of GS25’s signature dosirak since 2010. “We launched a renewal of GS25 dosirak earlier this month. We conduct consumer surveys, and the results show that consumers’ needs keep changing. We cannot create dosirak based solely on trends or what's popular in society. We need hard data that reflects consumers’ opinions,” Min said. GS25's dosirak featuring Kim Hye-ja, left, includes five main dishes, five sides and two appetizers. GS25's No.1 Chicken Dorisak features garlic mayo chicken and spicy garlic fried chicken. Courtesy of GS Retail Launching a new dosirak starts with analyzing current market trends and planning how to target consumers, followed by deciding on the banchan and style. Culinary experts test the selected dishes and adjust their flavors to create a balanced meal. The completed sample then undergoes a “lot test” at a manufacturing plant to determine whether it is suitable for mass production. Based on feedback from the test, the final dosirak is prepared for launch. Around 20 different types of dosirak are featured each month at GS25 stores. GS Retail runs nine manufacturing plants nationwide that together distribute dosirak to 18,000 GS25 stores across Korea. The key is consistent quality and taste for all dosirak products of the same type. Launching a new dosirak usually takes about 12 weeks. Some products, such as spring cabbage bibimbap, which went viral on social media, are produced more quickly by the company to take advantage of swift moving trends. Korean dosirak, according to Min, were heavily influenced by Japanese bento back when the domestic market was small and limited. For many years, there were not even proper food containers available in Korea. “But the market has grown, and now there are more than 53,000 convenience stores. There are diverse food containers and equipment to realize a greater variety of banchan for mass production. We have built up know-how like how to bake bread to soak up different sauces or how to make dried seaweed for triangular gimbap crispier,” Min said. “We’re trying to implement automation at our plants, except placing banchan in each container because robots take a longer time for that job than humans hand-packing them.”

title: GS Retail stock holds steady as investors watch recent earnings - AD HOC NEWS
content: GS Retail stock reflects recent earnings trends from the first half of 2026, giving investors a clearer view of its core retail and convenience business. The latest revenue and profit figures highlight both growth areas and margin pressures. GS Retail stock (ISIN KR7007070006) remains closely tied to the company’s recent earnings performance, with investors focusing on the most up-to-date revenue and profit figures from its latest reported period in 2026. As of September 20, 2026, the stock’s valuation is increasingly being viewed through the lens of these fundamentals and the broader consumer and retail environment in South Korea. For the most recent reported period in fiscal 2026, GS Retail disclosed consolidated revenue running in the hundreds of billions of KRW, underscoring the scale of its convenience store and retail operations. The latest half-year results for 2026 show that revenue for the period rose compared with the corresponding period of the prior year, reflecting both store network expansion and steady same-store sales growth. In that same reporting period, operating profit also increased versus the previous year, but at a slower pace than revenue, pointing to ongoing margin pressure from labor and logistics costs. The company’s earnings mix continues to be driven by its core convenience store segment, with food, beverage and daily-needs items accounting for the bulk of sales. Within these results, management highlighted revenue growth that outpaced the prior year by a mid-single-digit to high-single-digit percent range, while operating profit improved by a lower percent rate, illustrating the challenge of fully passing cost pressures on to consumers. Historical figures from fiscal year 2024 are now used mainly as a comparison base: in that year, GS Retail reported smaller revenue and operating profit levels than in the most recently reported 2026 period, indicating a multi-year growth trend but also showing that profit margins have not expanded in line with sales. For investors, operating margin in the latest 2026 reporting period is a key metric. The most recent figures show that operating margin remains in the low- to mid-single-digit percent range, constrained by higher input costs and ongoing investments in store refurbishment and digital services. Compared with the prior year’s margin, this represents only a modest improvement, underscoring that GS Retail’s growth is still largely volume-driven rather than margin-driven. Net profit for the most recent half-year in 2026 also increased versus the same period a year earlier, but the rise was smaller than the growth in revenue, reinforcing the picture of gradual, but not dramatic, earnings leverage. Management guidance for the remainder of fiscal 2026, as communicated alongside these latest results, points to a continued focus on cost discipline and selective store expansion. The company has indicated that it expects revenue for full-year 2026 to exceed the prior year’s level, while aiming for a slight improvement in operating margin compared with 2025. Historical guidance from fiscal year 2024 serves as a backdrop here: at that time, GS Retail’s outlook was for more moderate revenue growth and stable margins, and the subsequent actual results suggest that the company has managed to deliver somewhat better top-line momentum than originally signaled, though margin enhancement remains gradual. As of September 20, 2026, GS Retail’s market capitalization on its primary listing in South Korea reflects the cumulative impact of these earnings trends and expectations for the remainder of the year. The current valuation embeds assumptions of continued revenue growth in 2026 and a cautious improvement in profitability, with the convenience store segment remaining the central earnings driver. Compared with historical market capitalization levels in earlier years, the current figure stands higher, mirroring the company’s larger revenue base and expansion of its store network, though investors are still monitoring whether margins can improve enough to justify further rerating. From a longer-term perspective, GS Retail’s latest 2026 results and guidance suggest that the stock now trades on a balance between growth potential and cost-related risks. For investors, the most important checkpoint over the coming quarters will be whether operating margin can move meaningfully higher from its low- to mid-single-digit percent range as revenue continues to grow. If the company can demonstrate that its investments in logistics, digital platforms and store upgrades translate into better profitability, the current earnings trajectory in 2026 may support a more constructive view of GS Retail stock. title: A game developer bought a GeForce 8400 GS for $10 to find the absolute minimum. - GameGPU
content: A Reddit user shared their experience creating a very low-cost benchmark rig to test the compatibility of a game they were developing. To determine the absolute minimum hardware requirements, the developer purchased a discrete MSI GeForce 8400 GS graphics card for $10, including shipping and taxes. This graphics accelerator will serve as the lower performance benchmark for the train simulator, which is being developed using the Godot 4.4 engine and is designed to mimic the visual style of Microsoft Train Simulator and SimCity 4. The enthusiast's test configuration includes an AMD FX-6100 processor, an MSI N8400GS-D512D3H/LP graphics card with 512 MB of DDR3 memory at 1100 MHz and a GPU frequency of 520 MHz, a Creative Sound Blaster Audigy 1 sound card, 8 GB of DDR3 RAM, and a 64 GB SATA solid-state drive. All components are housed in a Rosewill Line-M case, and the base operating system for initial testing was Windows XP Professional x64. The project heavily utilizes the CPU, so the graphics adapter is the least demanding component in the system architecture. The main goal of the build is to test frame rate stability on legacy graphics solutions supporting basic OpenGL standards. A previous prototype of the project already demonstrated around 540 frames per second on an Intel Core i5-2400 and GeForce GT 640. The developer expects to achieve at least 30 frames per second on a GeForce 8400 GS, while reaching 60 frames per second will be the maximum optimization result for the chosen ultra-budget device class.
