title: The Underrated Lexus Cars That Deliver M-Car Character Without The BMW Repair Bill - HotCars
content: Henry Cesari is an automotive journalist and lifelong gearhead. His writing career began with his first newspaper article at age 15—the same year he inherited his first project car, a 1964 Dodge Dart. That slant-six-powered Mopar was an exceptionally forgiving teacher on the fundamentals of wrenching. And it sparked a lifelong fascination with the forgotten machines, engineering oddities, and the human stories behind technology. Since then, Henry has spent two decades writing about cars, the people who keep them alive, and travel in general. As a freelancer, a staff writer at MotorBiscuit, and features writer at HotCars, he has covered the automotive industry from inside Detroit, attending press events, interviewing industry figures, reviewing new products, and digging into the local history behind obscure enthusiast vehicles. Subscribe to the HotCars newsletter to never miss an update There are two moments when owning a BMW makes perfect sense. The first is when the road bends. The second is when you sell it before another expensive part breaks. That second joke is a little unfair: Modern BMWs are actually among the most reliable cars Consumer Reports tracks. But reliability and cheap ownership aren’t the same thing. So what if you want the steering, balance, power, and general troublemaking spirit of a BMW M car without quite so much fear of the eventual repair bill?     Lexus built an entire lineup that looks like a very good deal on the used market. What do die-hard fans love about their BMW sports cars? At their very best, these vehicles feel as if their every element is engineered around the driver. Steering, seating position, chassis balance, and traditional engine layout just keep pulling enthusiasts back to the Bavarian brand. Consumer Reports currently ranks BMW second among all automakers, first among luxury brands, first in road tests, and second in owner satisfaction. The only drivers who love their cars more are Subaru owners. Critics often joke that a finicky BMW spends every weekend on a tow truck. Nothing could be further from the truth. Consumer Reports also analyzed about 380,000 vehicles for its latest reliability survey and gave BMW a 58/100 predicted-reliability score. That landed it in fifth overall and made it the only European brand in the top 10. Lexus eked out a win with a 60/100 score. The question that keeps BMW owners up at night is, “What happens when this wonderfully complicated machine does finally break down?” And to be blunt, the BMW company is making the answer uglier with every new generation of vehicles it builds. The numbers don’t lie. Consumer Reports currently ranks BMW 25th for maintenance and repair cost, while Lexus lands at 15th. What’s the damage? RepairPal’s current Reliability Rating covers 2010–2019 model-year vehicles and puts the average BMW’s annual unscheduled repair and maintenance cost at $968, versus $551 for Lexus. The difference is substantial. BMW locks increasingly ordinary jobs behind paid information, diagnostic software, registration procedures, and specialized equipment. Want to replace the battery on a recent BMW yourself? You can, but on many modern BMWs the job isn’t finished until you electronically register the new battery with the car using compatible diagnostic software. Many of the automaker's recent cars did away with the dipstick altogether in favor of electronic oil level monitoring, a system that has since suffered software issues. Need access to the software to attempt your own repairs? A portal to BMW’s Technical Information System costs $32 for one day, $270 for a month, or $2,700 for a year. No wonder small independent shops must charge high prices to repair your car. On the other hand, if you buy an old Lexus you’re buying into Toyota’s enormous mass-market ecosystem, with related engines, parts, and procedures familiar to many Toyota and Lexus independent mechanics. Sure, BMW has MINI, but there’s far less overlap with a giant mainstream lineup. That gives the aging Lexus a broader service ecosystem before you even get into the parts bill. Lexus didn't build a single halo car to lure away BMW drivers; it took on the entire M car lineup with its F car family. The 416-hp Lexus IS F arrived for 2008 to take on the V8 M3, the 467-hp Lexus RC F dove into M4 territory, and the 467-hp Lexus GS F gave the M5 a naturally aspirated alternative. RepairPal’s published model-level estimates illustrate the value proposition on the used market: $531 a year for an older IS F versus $1,161 for the M3; $754 for the RC F versus $2,781 for the M4; and $499 for the GS F versus $1,173 for the M5. RepairPal says it lacks enough data to issue formal reliability ratings for most of these low-volume models, so treat those numbers as estimates, not gospel. But the broader brand data points the same direction: Lexus led J.D. Power’s 2026 Vehicle Dependability Study with 151 problems per 100 vehicles. Consider one direct comparison. The short-lived V8-powered M3 is notorious because its rod bearings can fail catastrophically, destroying the engine. On the other hand, the IS F’s 2UR-GSE is a naturally aspirated 5.0-liter V8. It belongs to Toyota’s UR V8 family, sharing the 94-mm bore architecture of the 4.6-liter 1UR but stretching the stroke to 89.5 mm for a 5.0-liter displacement, with forged hardware and Yamaha-engineered performance cylinder heads. Its closest Toyota-badged 2UR cousin powered the Century luxury sedan, while 4.6-liter UR relatives served in Tundras and Land Cruisers. It has a reputation for running forever. When Lexus created the RC F, engineers essentially kept the IS F cylinder block while replacing most other parts, and increasing output from 416 to 467 horsepower. The GS F received the same 467-hp basic recipe, and even the non-F LC 500 later used the 2UR-GSE. And yes, the Lexus V8 still has a dipstick. Repairability gets even more intriguing at the bottom of the lineup. The 2018–2023 IS 350 uses the same 2GR-FKS 3.5-liter V6 engine designation as the contemporary Tacoma. Of course, it's tuned for speed, not tow rating: the IS 350 raises horsepower from the Tacoma's 278 to 311. In short, this is a nimble, compact luxury sports sedan built around the engine block from Toyota's midsize pickup. No, the Lexus F cars aren’t exactly like BMW’s M series. When evaluating the RC F, Consumer Reports lined one up against the BMW M4. Reviewers found the Lexus heavier and a little less sharp. They did praise its firm, direct steering and relentless speed. But in many comparisons, BMW still owns the final few percent of the sports-sedan magic. Lexus prioritized a slightly different experience. The RC F sends a 467-hp naturally aspirated V8 through an eight-speed automatic and available torque-vectoring differential, while the GS F uses the same horsepower figure and a standard torque-vectoring rear differential. But the lineup isn’t all about straight-line speed. Lexus developed the IS F and GS F on circuits including the Nürburgring. They are all serious rear-drive performance cars. The Lexus F cars aren’t just Toyotas with some extra chrome, either. They’re luxury machines. Consumer Reports described the RC F as giving up a little performance in exchange for enough comfort to become a better daily driver than harder-edged alternatives. Factor in the repair-cost spread already examined, and the Lexus starts to look less like the consolation prize for refusing to buy an M car and more like a deliberately different answer to the same question. iSeeCars analyzed more than 395 million vehicles and estimates the average Lexus has a 14.4% chance of reaching 250,000 miles. That makes it 4.2 times as likely as the average luxury vehicle to reach 250,000 miles. In fact, it ranked second among all brands, regular or luxury, imported or domestic. BMW lags far behind with 0.5%. In addition to lasting ridiculously long, Lexus cars have one more advantage that may make them collectible soon. Hagerty’s 2024 survey found 60% of Gen Z respondents interested in owning a classic car. The "classic" they most often inquired about insuring was the NA Mazda Miata. Of the five additional vehicles the generation is already asking about that older drivers seem to be ignoring, 80% are Japanese. No German machines made the cut. I understand the BMW owner’s affliction: I drive one daily. There’s just something about my car that makes the inevitable next repair feel like tomorrow’s problem. Today's problem is hunting for the next empty on-ramp. But immortality will go to the performance cars that remain usable, repairable, and desirable for so long after their warranties expire that they’re worth fully restoring. The Lexus F cars may have been playing the longer game all along. Sources: Consumer Reports, J.D. Power, BMW Group, Lexus, Toyota, RepairPal, iSeeCars, Hagerty We want to hear from you.
